title: Casper and the Portrait
premise: Property surveyor Odile Delacroix takes a routine appraisal of the Harrow house in rural Vermont, where the frost patterns on the windows form names and the sleep recordings capture a second voice answering questions Odile never asked aloud. The voice belongs to Etienne Harrow, a boy taken by his family in 1974 and never reported missing, and the house will not let Odile leave until what was taken — Etienne's body, hidden in the well — is returned to the ground and named. As the frost writes its final pattern across every window, Odile must choose between the law that says the property belongs to a bank and the justice the house demands: a burial, a headstone, a name spoken aloud. The house releases them only when the town itself is forced to remember what it agreed to forget.
about_author: Wren Lockridge is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade walking through houses that had outlived their owners. They write horror about the debts buildings keep, from a farmhouse in the Champlain Valley.

chapters.title: The Square Footage of Silence
chapters.summary: Odile Delacroix arrives to appraise the Harrow house, measuring rooms that measure back — tape reels drifting, doorways a half-inch narrower on the return. They keep their professional rituals: lights on, doors counted, exits logged. The beat is unease dressed as competence; Odile trusts procedure the way other people trust people.

chapters.title: Frost, in a Hand You Recognize
chapters.summary: Overnight frost blooms on every window in identical cursive: a name, Etienne, repeated until the glass cracks. Odile photographs it, files it as vandalism, but the pattern reappears inside the sealed attic. POV Odile, with the emotional beat of a professional's certainty beginning to splinter.

chapters.title: Questions in the Dark
chapters.summary: Odile leaves a recorder running during sleep, a habit from a bad year. Playback captures a second voice — a child's — answering questions Odile doesn't remember asking: Are you the one who counts? Do they know where I am? The beat is violation; the house has been inside their sleep.

chapters.title: What the Deed Doesn't Say
chapters.summary: At the county records office, Odile finds the 1974 deed transfer and a newspaper clipping: the Harrow family left overnight, one son unaccounted for, no report filed. The clerk goes pale at the name. POV shifts to the clerk, Marguerite, whose mother was a Harrow neighbor — the beat is complicity inherited like furniture.

chapters.title: The Well Has a Sound
chapters.summary: Following the frost's direction, Odile finds a capped well behind the collapsed greenhouse; lowering a phone on a rope, they record water, then breathing, then a voice finishing a sentence begun fifty years ago. The beat is dread tipping into obligation — Odile understands the house isn't haunting them, it's hiring them.

chapters.title: Everyone Knew the Shape of the Family
chapters.summary: Marguerite confronts her dying mother, who confesses the town helped the Harrows leave quietly after what the father did, and that no one asked about the boy because asking would have cost everyone. POV Marguerite; the beat is the sick relief of a secret finally spoken and the shame that follows it.

chapters.title: The House Appraises Back
chapters.summary: The bank orders Odile to finalize the appraisal; the house answers by repricing every room in frost — each valuation a date, each date a night Etienne waited. Doors Odile counted now open onto rooms that weren't there. The beat is escalation: procedure can no longer contain what the house is demanding.

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Four
chapters.summary: Sleeping in the house one last time, Odile is pulled fully into the recordings — into the winter of 1974, walking the halls as Etienne, hearing the family pack and drive away, hearing the well lid close. The beat is terror transmuted into grief; Odile returns knowing exactly what was taken and by whom.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Odile and Marguerite open the well in the first hard frost and bring up small remains. The town's sheriff arrives to stop them — no permit, no jurisdiction — but Marguerite stands on the law's side of the line for the first time, and neighbors arrive with shovels. The beat is the climax: justice assembled outside the law, in the open, in daylight.

chapters.title: The Final Pattern
chapters.summary: They bury Etienne Harrow under a stone with his name and dates, and the whole town speaks them aloud. The frost writes one last pattern across every window — thank you — and then never again. Odile files the appraisal at fair value and leaves the lights on. The beat is belonging: a house at rest, and two people who finally count their doors out of habit, not fear.
